text: yeah this one was always in the planning. the worry is forward contamination, dropping microbes or debris onto an ocean world like Enceladus while the probe is still active. so the final dive into Saturn’s atmosphere was basically a clean kill. it burns up instead of sitting out there as a possible contaminant. I remember this being a deliberate part of the mission endgame, not just an accident. not sure about the exact odds, but the point stands: you don’t let a spacecraft that has seen lots of space just hang around where it could hit a promising moon.

yeah this happens to me on longer rides, but if you’re standing on one leg on the board while the other one pushes, that standing leg basically has to hold your whole weight and keep the board steady at the same time. so the quads, hamstrings and calves are working really hard just to not wobble. a buddy of mine swears by it, keep your weight centered and don’t lock your knees. it’s a mix of the muscle staying tense for too long and the repeated little impacts from the wheels hitting the ground. also if you’re gripping the board too hard, you can pull on yourself and get pulled out of line, which makes the standing leg do extra work to recover balance.

tbh, most of my skate sessions end with my back leg sore for a couple of days. I mostly ride with one leg staying on the board while the other pushes, and after a while the aching shows up. I don’t know if that’s normal for everyone, but it’s something I get used to. the trick, I guess, is to keep your weight more over the board and let the pushing leg do the work, instead of having the stationary leg take all the strain. also, if you’re gripping too tight or leaning one way, your other leg ends up doing double work just to stay upright.

and yeah, the uneven pavement makes it worse. every little bump sends a jolt up that leg, and if your muscles are already tired from holding still, they don’t recover between hits. I used to think it was just part of skating, but my knee started complaining too, so I slowed down and started focusing on a relaxed, centered stance. the pain didn’t disappear, but it’s less constant now.

It’s easy to trip over the name because “African American” sounds like it’s describing where someone currently lives, but it’s really an identity term about ancestral roots. Black Americans were often descendants of enslaved people from West and Central Africa, so the “African” part is pointing at that heritage. The term gained traction in the 1960s as part of Black American self-identification, and it’s less about someone being a resident of Africa and more about shared cultural and historical ties to Africa.

A lot of Black Americans aren’t “from Africa” in the everyday sense, but “African American” is shorthand for a diaspora identity. I get why it feels misleading. It doesn’t mean every one of them was born in or recently moved from Africa. My grandpa always said that Black families here carry a lot of West African cultural roots even when nobody can point to a single homeland. And yes, some Black Americans are direct immigrants from Africa, but the label was never meant to be a passport check. It’s really a heritage marker, not a current address. Most people say African American, and the Afro-American spelling is the older variant.

ok so the thing with opioids is that they are not like candy. They bind to receptors in the brain and slow things down, so you get euphoria and pain relief but also slower breathing. That tradeoff is the point. Your body is built to keep things stable, and a strong push toward pleasure or calm creates a pushback. That pushback is where adverse effects come from. Tolerance is the obvious one. Your brain stops responding the same way after repeated use, so people need more for the same feeling. Withdrawal shows the body trying to rebalance, which is why stopping after long use can feel awful. I have felt this happen to me.

For stimulants like cocaine, the hit comes from flooding the brain with dopamine, and the body responds by adjusting how much dopamine it produces. That adjustment is the start of dependence. You can also get headaches or dry mouth, and the cardiovascular system gets stressed. With alcohol, the liver has to process it, and the brain gets slowed, which is why coordination and judgment go down. When someone asks why all drugs are bad, the word bad is doing a lot of work. Drugs are not automatically bad and strong psychoactive effects almost always mean the body has to compensate. Compensation is the adverse effect, whether that is tolerance or withdrawal.

There is also individual variation. Some people handle alcohol poorly, others seem fine. If a drug gives intense euphoria, it is reaching deep into reward pathways. Those pathways touch breathing and mood, so zero adverse effects would mean it only hits the pleasure button and nothing else, which is basically a fantasy. Low dose use or careful selection of drugs avoids the bad parts sometimes, but intense pleasure is the part that usually comes with cost.

The honest answer is that the brain does not separate pleasure from the rest of the body. If a substance flips the reward system hard enough to feel great, it is also changing baseline chemistry, and the body will try to correct that. That correction is what people experience as bad effects, whether mild or severe. So no drug gives you the same intense high with zero tradeoffs. Most people looking for a magic high are asking for the upside without the biological bill, and biology rarely gives you a free ride. It is that kind of bill you pay.

Hi there,

Honestly this is a pretty common slip. When you ask someone what cows drink, the strongest word that comes to mind is usually milk, because we constantly pair cows with milk. That strong association can beat the less obvious answer, especially if your attention is already tied up with the silly “silk” repetition. So the spelling task probably filled up your working memory, and your brain went with the default association instead of the correct fact. You weren't being stubborn; your mind grabbed the most familiar cow association under load. It's just how memory shortcuts work: familiar pairings jump out before slower, more accurate retrieval. If it happens a lot or comes with other slips, maybe you're tired, distracted, or worth a quick check. If you want, try the reverse: name animals that drink water. You'll find the correct answer comes more easily with practice.

Take care,
Me

Hey,

yeah I get why this is confusing. The 3-in-1 is one formula trying to do three jobs, so it works less well at each than separate products. It has to clean your hair, clean your skin, and leave hair feeling conditioned. That means the surfactants and conditioning agents have to compromise across body and hair. A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner is only trying to handle hair, so it's simpler. The 3-in-1 adds bodywash to that mix, and that changes how the shampoo and conditioner parts perform.

For me it's fine for short hair or when I need one bottle for travel. I've used them on a few weekends where I wanted less to pack, and they were okay, but not the kind I'd use daily. On longer hair or fine hair it can feel undercleaned or not soft enough, so I usually reach for separate products. It's the compromise that matters: you're trading some effectiveness for one bottle and less stuff in the bag. The smell is the least reliable part too, because one scent has to cover both skin and hair. For the bag I'd use it, for daily I'd split products.

not sure about the gym bag vs routine though.

Hey Sam,

Good question. The short version is that GPS is the main tool. Surveyors install GPS stations right on the land, and they take position readings repeatedly over months or years. Each station gives you an x, y, z coordinate, and if you compare the numbers from 2005 to today you can see a tiny shift. On the North American Plate, that shift works out to something like a couple of millimeters a year, which is slow but measurable.

The tricky bit is the math. You don't just look at one station. You compare stations far apart to separate the whole plate moving from local ground movement like settling or earthquakes. Then you get a velocity vector, basically direction plus speed. That is what people mean when they say the continent is moving at a few millimeters per year. It is not a single measurement, it is a long campaign of positions that you fit together.

I've seen this used for tectonic plates and for local uplift in mountain regions. If you want, I can point you to a public GPS dataset next.

New colleagues often wonder why inbreeding can be linked to lower average IQ. Inbreeding between closely related parents makes it more likely that both carry the same rare or harmful recessive genetic variants. Those variants can stay hidden for generations in mixed populations, but become more apparent when related people have children. IQ is not controlled by one gene; many genes each contribute a little. When a child inherits two copies of a mildly unfavorable allele, that can slightly reduce cognitive development. The bigger problem is that inbreeding increases the chance of rare recessive disorders, and those health effects can affect the brain or overall development. It is a population-level pattern, not a guarantee for every family, and the degree of relatedness matters. The main science is increased homozygosity: related parents are more likely to pass the same recessive alleles, so harmful variants hidden in ancestors may appear in offspring.

You may have noticed that arm injuries are often described as less painful than injuries to the ribs, spine, or face. That is not a fixed rule, but there is an anatomical reason behind the general impression.

The upper arm has a lot of muscle and a good blood supply. It also has major nerves running through it, but those nerves are more spread out than in some other body parts. Injuries to the ribs, for example, can hit bone, pleura, or intercostal nerves, and that combination tends to be very painful. The spine and face have dense nerve networks and vital structures, so even small injuries there can be quite uncomfortable.

The arm is also an appendage, so moving it is usually less restricted than, say, a rib injury. That said, a deep cut, a broken humerus, or a nerve injury in the arm can still hurt a great deal. Pain is personal, and the exact spot, depth, and type of injury matter a lot.

Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas, which already makes it hard to detect. The main reason it is so poisonous is that it attaches to hemoglobin in the blood with very high affinity, roughly two hundred times stronger than oxygen does. That bound form is called carboxyhemoglobin. Because hemoglobin is occupied, the blood carries less oxygen to tissues, so the body's cells are starved of oxygen even if the air still contains plenty of oxygen. Carbon dioxide is not dangerous through the same pathway. It is not a strong competitor for hemoglobin, so normal breathing expels it as a waste product. High concentrations of carbon dioxide can still be harmful because too much can depress the central nervous system or displace oxygen, but that is different from carbon monoxide's chemical trapping of oxygen transport.

Practically, low levels of carbon monoxide can cause headaches, dizziness, and confusion; higher levels can lead to loss of consciousness and, if untreated, organ damage. That is why it is treated as an acute poison rather than a normal respiratory gas. The key difference is therefore not that CO2 is harmless under all conditions, but that CO2 does not lock onto hemoglobin in the same way. It is produced by metabolism and normally removed by the lungs without needing to be chemically bound to proteins. Carbon monoxide, by contrast, can accumulate in the blood during incomplete combustion, car exhaust, or faulty heating equipment, and because it is invisible and smell-free, people may inhale it for a long time before noticing. In practice, this is why enclosed spaces with poor ventilation are the most common setting for CO exposure. For a colleague without a science background, the short version is that CO blocks oxygen transport in the blood, whereas CO2 is simply a byproduct that the body exhales.

When an aircraft hits the ground or another object, our bodies keep moving forward because of momentum, and that motion is what causes injury. The brace position reduces that forward and upward movement. You get low, keep your head back against the seat, and pull your arms down and back. This shortens the distance you travel inside the cabin before you stop, and it keeps your face and head from being thrown into the seat, floor or overhead.

The idea is simple: an object in motion stays in motion unless something stops it. In a collision, the aircraft stops, but passengers do not stop instantly. The brace position gives your body a shorter path to stop and aligns your limbs so forces spread across larger muscle groups. That reduces the load on your neck, spine and internal organs. It also keeps you from becoming a projectile that hits seats or walls. If you are not braced, your head, chest and legs can strike fixed cabin surfaces. Bracing puts you in a position that lets those surfaces stop you less violently. It is not a guarantee of safety, but in a serious impact it can lower the severity of injuries.

A lot of people think the industrial revolution created the first big companies, but there were trading houses and banks like the Medici and the Dutch East India Company. What changed was scale. Before factories and railways, most businesses stayed local or depended on a small network. They were often family-run, limited by how much people could carry and store. Industrialization brought mass production, faster communication, and a corporate structure that let firms grow far beyond one founder or one region. So the old firms weren’t unknown, they just didn’t have the same reach that makes modern brands instantly recognizable.

I actually went through this last year, so I have a pretty specific memory of it. The car I was looking at had a “special rate” from the dealer that looked amazing on paper. I was ready to say yes before I saw the full breakdown, and then I noticed the financing was bundled with extended warranty, service plan, and a gap coverage product. The interest rate was lower, sure, but the total payment was higher than when I took the same car to my bank. That’s the thing with dealership financing: the low rate is often a lure, and the extras get wrapped in quietly.

I keep thinking about that showroom moment because it feels like a trap set for people who only compare interest rates. I asked the dealer to strip out the add-ons and the “cheap” financing became less cheap. The bank gave me a slightly higher rate, but no bundled products, and my total cost of credit came out lower. So my position is straightforward: the sticker rate is only one number, and the package is what determines whether the bank is actually cheaper.

For me it came down to how much of the total cost is hidden. Dealership financing often includes a stack of optional products, and sometimes you can’t tell until you ask for the itemized breakdown. Bank financing is more straightforward: you get the loan terms, and you pay for anything else only if you choose to. That’s why, despite the lower dealer rate, the bank ended up costing me less overall.

I also found it annoying how quickly the dealer’s numbers changed when I pushed back. That’s a concrete detail I remember, and it mattered more than any single interest rate. I think that’s the real reason: the bank isn’t winning on rate, it’s winning on total package cost. I’m not saying dealers always pad the price, but I would never again sign a loan just because the headline rate looked better.

I’d also mention that dealer financing sometimes assumes you’ll buy the car through them and take their add-ons, while a bank loan can be used for the same car without those extras. I found that distinction helpful when I was comparing offers. It’s the kind of thing that’s easy to miss if you’re focused on the rate alone. I was tempted to take the dealer offer because the rate was low, but the total was the real comparison point.

So my take is simple: lower dealer interest rates can be misleading because the total package cost often ends up higher. The bank may have a higher rate but fewer hidden extras, and that can make it cheaper in practice. I learned that by watching the total, not just the rate.

The patchwork mess of marijuana legality works for me, tbh. In California I can walk into a dispensary and buy a joint like it's milk, but driving home over the Nevada line turns my ride into a legal headache. That part drives me nuts. I don't think one national law makes sense because states are really different: Oregon is way more relaxed than Texas, and Colorado's tax system funds school programs. If every state copied one rule, small towns would lose choices they've already voted for. The only fix I'd make is clear interstate rules, so people aren't guessing whether a bag of weed is legal in the car. I get the fear that states are experimenting and making a mess. But I've seen friends get caught crossing state lines with flowers, and I'd rather have that problem. Until then, it's another American contradiction, and I'm fine with that.

yeah this one actually trips me up too because electricity here isn't like a power plant in your chest. it's ion flow across membranes. every cell pumps sodium out and potassium in with that ATPase enzyme, which sets up a voltage difference. when a neuron gets stimulated, sodium channels open, sodium rushes in, the membrane depolarizes, and that's the action potential. your heart's pacemaker cells do this automatically, which is why your heartbeat runs without you thinking about it, and muscles contract when their own sodium channels fire. honestly the whole thing is chemical electricity, not sparks, so the battery idea is kinda misleading.

I’ve been making music for long enough to have a take on sampling, and I’m going to be blunt: it’s the most creative shortcut in music, but also the most legally annoying. The actual process is simple to describe and harder to do well.

You start with the original recording, which is usually a vinyl pressing, a CD, or a digital file. You isolate the part you want — a two-bar loop of drums, a vocal hook, a chord progression — and drop it into your DAW. From there, you’re not just pasting it in. You chop it into slices, time-stretch or pitch-shift it, and layer it under your own production. The trick isn’t finding a cool snippet; it’s deciding what to keep, what to cut, and how to make it sit in a new context without it feeling like a guest that never got the invitation.

The legal side is where people get burned. In the US, using someone else’s master recording is a right, not a permission slip. You need clearance from the label that owns the master, and often from the songwriter’s publisher. Some artists get creative and clear everything; others bet on the “fair use” defense, which is a gamble courts don’t always win. I’ve seen tracks sit in a drawer for years over this, and I’ve seen others just pay the money and move on. My take: budget for it early, and never treat “I’ll fight it later” as a plan.

There’s also a craft argument for sampling: it lets you borrow a texture or a feel you can’t easily recreate. A 1970s funk loop has a groove that’s nearly impossible to program from scratch, and a chopped vocal can become a new melodic hook. But I think the best sampling isn’t lazy. It’s listening to the source until you understand why that snippet works, then shaping it deliberately. The worst sampling is grabbing a famous hook and letting it do all the work.

If I’m being honest, the most useful thing sampling teaches is restraint. You’re not assembling a playlist; you’re editing a piece of someone else’s music into your own. That difference is the whole game.

I got one last week after staring at this laptop for four hours, and for me it's almost always the tight neck and scalp thing, not some mysterious storm behind the eyes. The muscles get knotted up and that pressure starts to build until it aches. I think most "headaches" are just the brain telling you something is off, whether it's dehydration, poor posture, or too much screen.

I've had this happen when I skip water, and I also know a buddy who gets the same thing from chewing gum way too long. So yeah, it hurts because your body is literally flagging that things have been pushed past comfortable.

So I hit this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m. and honestly there was no line at all, which was weird. Our tab landed around $130 and that felt steep. Going in I figured it was about what you'd pay at a steakhouse, but then I found out it actually cost more than I expected for a steakhouse, so yeah.

The thing I was most disappointed about was no steak. At that price I really expected at least some kind of steak option. You got lamb, prime rib, and chicken though. My take is you can find that meat stuff at other Las Vegas buffets for way less.

The seafood station did have Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are all over Vegas buffets, but I hadn't seen rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were kinda interesting. The catch was no crab-cracker crackers. Staff mentioned wooden mallets, but our table was right up against the next one and I didn't want to start smashing shells and sending little pieces flying at the people beside us. Ended up just eating the crab legs.

The Asian station didn't strike me as very distinctive. Honestly it reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and pastries, but nothing really popped. Fresh juices were there too, though I didn't try any.

My overall call is that it's acceptable but overpriced for what you get. If you're curious it's fine to try once, especially when there's no wait. If there's a long line though, I'd probably think twice.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, mostly because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so “example” becomes “eexample” and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I’m typing fast and not looking.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don’t ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I’d have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I've gone to Vegas pretty much my whole life, the under 21 version of it, so I've sat through a bunch of shows before I could even gamble. Le Reve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe it's slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You're basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view, which is rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too, the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil, not exactly a rip-off, just, if you've seen Cirque, you've seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

The clarity is the problem. What's the story? I still don't know. There's a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it's trying to say. Also way too much is happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like that stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, where more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you're staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn't blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. Still, a few friends liked it, and if you've never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

so about two years ago we ordered two shirts for my dad from Rockmount Ranch Wear over the phone. the sales rep got the address wrong, her handwritten 7 was read as a 1. the right address was 5407 but the package went to 5401 and the shirts never arrived. the residents there took it to the local UPS store to return. then the package disappeared and nobody heard from it again. we found out several weeks later. while the dispute was going on we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. the owner handled it then, admitted the shipment went to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts were returned. he also said we were partly at fault for not being friendly enough to the 5401 folks four doors away. we disputed the original charge with our credit-card company and eventually got a credit. tbh we were annoyed by how long it took.
